entry: Artificial sea-level waterway in Egypt, connecting the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Red Sea]] across the Isthmus of Suez. Opened on November 17, 1869, the 193.3 km (120.1 mi) canal is a key trade route between Europe and Asia; in 2021, more than 20,600 vessels used it. It shortens the journey from the Arabian Sea to London by about 8,900 km (5,500 mi). The canal has no [[Lock (water navigation)|locks]], and seawater flows through it freely. European shareholders, mostly British and French, owned the operating company until 1956, when President [[Gamal Abdel Nasser|Nasser]] nationalized it, leading to the monthlong [[Suez Crisis]]. Under the Convention of Constantinople, the canal is open to commercial and war vessels in peace and war. Egypt closed it at the start of the [[Six-Day War]] in 1967, and it remained closed until 1975. Expansion in 2016 widened the Ballah Bypass and nearly doubled daily capacity, from 49 to 97 ships.

British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt in 1956. Israel invaded on October 29 to reopen the Straits of Tiran, and Britain and France joined on October 31 to depose President [[Gamal Abdel Nasser|Nasser]] and regain the [[Suez Canal]], which he had nationalized earlier that year. Heavy pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the [[United Nations|UN]] forced their withdrawal. The canal was closed from October 1956 to March 1957. The crisis strengthened Nasser's standing and humiliated Britain and France during the [[Cold War]]. The UN created an emergency force to police the Egypt–Israel border.

Unpleasant experience of aversion, usually linked to the perception of harm or threat of harm. Suffering is the basic element of negative [[Emotion|emotional]] states, opposed to [[Pleasure]] and [[Happiness]]. It is often categorized as physical or mental and ranges from mild to intolerable, with duration and frequency compounding intensity. Attitudes toward it vary according to whether it is seen as avoidable, useful, or deserved. Many fields study its nature, causes, and remedies. In Hellenistic philosophy, Cynics sought relief through self-sufficiency and indifference to life's vicissitudes, while Pyrrhonists held that suffering comes from dogmas, especially the belief that things are good or bad by nature. Neuroscience links suffering to brain networks, including the anterior cingulate cortex and insula, that turn raw [[Pain|pain]] into aversive motivation.

Right to vote in public political elections and referendums, also called the political franchise. Active suffrage is the right to vote, and passive suffrage is the right to stand for election; together they are sometimes called full suffrage. In most [[Democracy|democracies]], eligible voters elect representatives. [[Switzerland]] allows referendums at all levels of government, while they are rare in the [[United Kingdom]]. Suffrage remains restricted by age, residency, and citizenship in many places, and felons may lose the right to vote in Great Britain and the [[United States]]. Historically, voting was also limited by gender, race, or wealth. The short-lived Corsican Republic (1755–1769) was the first state to grant limited universal suffrage, to citizens over age 25. [[Women's suffrage]] was first granted nationally in [[New Zealand]] in 1893.

Diverse Islamic spiritual and ethical discipline concerned with spiritual excellence, purification of the self, and closeness to [[God]]. It also centers on remembrance of God (dhikr). Often described as [[Mysticism|mysticism]] within [[Islam]], a label that scholar Nile Green argues captures only one dimension; he prefers "a tradition of powerful knowledge, practices and persons." Sufis helped spread Islam through missionary and educational work. Most remain [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]], though some strands of Sufi thought entered [[Shia Islam]] in the late Middle Ages after the Safavid conversion of [[Iran]]. Mainstream Sufis observed Islamic law while opposing dry legalism. Sufi orders declined in the modern era under attacks from fundamentalist movements, but the tradition has revived in recent decades.

American professional boxer who competed from 1940 to 1965. Born Walker Smith Jr., he fought as an amateur under another boxer's identification card, and a remark that he was "sweet as sugar" gave him his ring name. Robinson held the world welterweight title from 1946 to 1951 and won the middleweight title in 1951. He was the first boxer to win a divisional world championship five times, including regaining the middleweight title from Carmen Basilio in 1958. His 91-fight unbeaten streak ran from 1943 to 1951, and he idolized [[Joe Louis]] as a youth. The International Boxing Research Organization ranked him the best pound-for-pound boxer of all time in 2006 and 2019. He was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990 and struggled financially after retiring in 1965.

Plant grown commercially for sugar, whose root contains a high concentration of [[Sucrose|sucrose]]. It is a cultivar group of the common beet (*Beta vulgaris*), closely related to [[Beetroot|beetroot]] and chard. Sugar beets grow in climates too cold for [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]], and in 2024 Russia and Germany were the largest producers in a world total of 294 million tonnes. The root is about 75% water and 20% sugar. [[Frederick the Great]], king of Prussia, subsidized experiments in [[Silesia]] in the mid-18th century, and in 1747 Andreas Marggraf isolated sugar from beetroots. Franz Karl Achard opened the first beet sugar factory in 1801, at Kunern in Silesia. Later [[Plant breeding|breeding]] raised sucrose content to around 18%, from about 5% to 6% in 1800.

Small nocturnal [[Marsupial|marsupial]] that glides between trees, *Petaurus breviceps*. It is omnivorous and eats sap, nectar and insects, a preference that gives it its common name. Gliding membranes called patagia stretch between its forelegs and hindlegs, letting it cover distances to reach food and escape predators. Strictly defined, the species is native to southern [[Queensland]] and most of [[New South Wales]], east of the [[Great Dividing Range]]. A wider species group occupies coastal eastern and northern Australia and [[New Guinea]]. Members of the genus are popular exotic pets.

Tall perennial grass of the genus *Saccharum*, grown for its sucrose-rich stalks. Sugarcane belongs to the [[Poaceae|grass family]], and its stalks reach 2–7 m (6–20 ft). It was domesticated in [[New Guinea]], and Austronesian sailors carried it to Polynesia, Madagascar and India. By the eighth century it was a luxury spice traded across the Mediterranean. Plantations in the 18th-century [[Caribbean]] drove large migrations of indentured and enslaved laborers. Sugarcane is the world's largest crop by production, at 1.9 billion tonnes in 2020, with [[Brazil]] producing 40%. It accounts for 79% of the world's sugar, and most of the rest comes from [[Sugar beet|sugar beets]]. Byproducts include [[Molasses]] and [[Biofuel|biofuel]].

American former record executive and co-founder of Death Row Records. Knight was central to the commercial success of gangsta rap in the 1990s, with the label's early hits by [[Dr. Dre]], *The Chronic* (1992), and [[Snoop Dogg]], *Doggystyle* (1993). He signed [[Tupac Shakur]] to the label after posting his $1.4 million bail in October 1995. In September 1996, Shakur was fatally wounded and Knight injured when an assailant fired into Knight's car in [[Las Vegas]]. In 2018 Knight pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter in a fatal 2015 hit-and-run and was sentenced to 28 years in prison.

Indonesian military general and second president, 1967–1998. After troops under his command countered an attempted coup on September 30 and October 1, 1965, the army carried out a nationwide anti-communist purge. Suharto became acting president in 1967 and president the following year. When he took power, [[Inflation|inflation]] exceeded 650%; his economic advisers adopted free-market policies, and prices were stable by 1969. In 1975 he ordered the invasion of East Timor, followed by a 23-year occupation. His New Order regime was an [[Authoritarianism|authoritarian]] state built around a [[Cult of personality|cult of personality]], and it drew Western backing during the [[Cold War]]. GDP grew by about 7% a year, and in 1986 the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization awarded him the Ceres Medal for rice self-sufficiency. Suharto resigned in May 1998 amid the 1997 Asian financial crisis. He is praised for economic growth and stability and condemned for corruption and human rights abuses.

Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 581 to 618. The Sui reunified China after the [[Northern and Southern dynasties]] era, ending centuries of division since the War of the Eight Princes. Founded by [[Emperor Wen of Sui|Emperor Wen]], it laid much of the institutional foundation for the [[Tang dynasty]], which succeeded it. Reforms included an equal-field land system, a Five Departments and Six Boards administration, and standardized coinage; the Sui also promoted [[Buddhism]]. The capital moved from Daxing (modern [[Xi'an]]) to [[Luoyang]] in 605. Massive projects included the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]], which linked Luoyang with the south, and the reconstruction of Luoyang, built with conscripted labor. Campaigns against Goguryeo in Korea failed by 614. Popular revolts followed, and Emperor Yang was assassinated in 618. The dynasty lasted only 37 years.

Means by which a person dies or attempts to die by suicide. Worldwide, [[Hanging|hanging]], [[Pesticide|pesticide]] poisoning, and [[Firearm|firearms]] predominate, though the pattern varies by country. Removing access to these means can prevent suicides, and gun-control measures in several countries have reduced suicides and gun deaths. Firearms have the highest case fatality rate, around 90%, with hanging at roughly 85%. In the [[United States]], firearms account for over half of suicides. Other measures include treatment of [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]], policies addressing alcohol misuse, and talk therapies such as dialectical behavior therapy.

Set of matching jacket and trousers of identical [[Textile|textile]], a Western dress garment. A suit is usually worn with a collared shirt, a necktie and dress shoes, and may include a waistcoat. The lounge suit originated in 19th-century Britain as country and sports clothing, which made it more casual than city dress. Its roots lie in early modern Western European court and military dress. In the 17th century, Charles II's English court adopted a long coat, waistcoat, cravat, [[Wig|wig]], knee breeches and [[Hat|hat]], following the example of [[Louis XIV]] at Versailles. In the early 20th century the suit replaced the black frock coat as regular daywear. Since the 1960s most suits have been mass-produced ready-to-wear garments, while bespoke suits are tailor-made from the client's measurements.

Indonesian statesman and first president, 1945–1967. Sukarno, with Mohammad Hatta, proclaimed independence on August 17, 1945, after Japan's surrender in [[World War II]]. He led resistance to Dutch efforts to reassert colonial rule until the Netherlands recognized Indonesian independence in 1949. In 1959 he introduced "Guided Democracy," an authoritarian system meant to restore stability and suppress regional rebellions. He positioned Indonesia as a leader of the [[Non-Aligned Movement]], which brought it closer to the [[Soviet Union]] despite its non-communist state. His plan for a rival United Nations based in [[Jakarta]] was the culmination of that policy. After an attempted coup in 1965 that was blamed on the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI), General [[Suharto]] took control, and Sukarno was placed under house arrest until his death.

Island in Indonesia, the world's eleventh-largest, also known as Celebes, a name first recorded in 1512 from Portuguese explorers. It covers 186,064.34 sq km (71,840 sq mi) including minor islands, and has four peninsulas separated by three gulfs. The Strait of Makassar separates it from [[Borneo]] to the west, and the [[Maluku Islands]] lie to the east. Its mountainous interior and northern volcanoes, such as Mount Lokon, reflect terranes from the Asian and Australian plates. Various [[Fault (geology)|faults]] make the island prone to [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], including deadly quakes in 2018 and 2021. Its peninsulas have traditionally been remote from each other and better connected by sea than by road.

Polyatomic anion, SO₄²⁻, found in salts of [[Sulfuric acid]]. Its sulfur atom sits at the center of four equivalent oxygen atoms in a [[Tetrahedral molecular geometry|tetrahedral]] arrangement, as predicted by VSEPR theory. Sulfate is the conjugate base of hydrogensulfate (HSO₄⁻). Organic sulfate esters, such as dimethyl sulfate, are covalent compounds. Sulfate salts, acid derivatives and peroxides are widely used in industry, and [[Gypsum|gypsum]] (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is a common sulfate mineral. IUPAC recommends the spelling "sulfate"; "sulphate" is traditional in British English. Bonding has been debated: [[Linus Pauling]] proposed double bonds using d orbitals in [[Valence bond theory]], but later work found d-orbital involvement less significant than he believed.

Nonmetallic [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol S and atomic number 16. It is the tenth most abundant element in the universe and the fifth most common on Earth, usually found in sulfide and [[Sulfate|sulfate]] minerals. Known since ancient times, it is also called brimstone, meaning "burning stone." Most elemental sulfur is recovered as a byproduct of removing sulfur from [[Natural gas|natural gas]] and [[Petroleum|petroleum]]. Its greatest use is in making [[Sulfuric acid]] for fertilizers. Sulfur is essential to life, as part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine and the vitamins biotin and thiamine. Its most common allotrope, cyclo-S₈, is a bright yellow solid that melts at 115.21 °C (239.38 °F).

Colorless, pungent gas, SO₂, a [[Chemical compound|chemical compound]] of sulfur and oxygen. It is released by volcanoes and produced by burning fossil fuels and by metals refining, with most output used to make [[Sulfuric acid]]. It is somewhat toxic when inhaled in large quantities for several minutes, and it is a precursor of [[Acid rain]]. On Venus it is the third most abundant atmospheric gas, at 150 ppm. The atmosphere of [[Io (moon)|Io]], a moon of [[Jupiter]], is 90% sulfur dioxide.

Colorless, odorless, viscous mineral acid, H₂SO₄, known in antiquity as oil of vitriol. It is hygroscopic and readily absorbs [[Water vapor|water vapor]]. Concentrated acid is a strong oxidant and dehydrating agent, corrosive to rocks and metals, and it can cause severe chemical [[Burn|burns]]. Adding water to the acid releases heat that can boil the solution, so the acid is added to water instead. Most of it is used to make [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], especially phosphates, and it is also important in mineral processing, oil refining and wastewater treatment. It is a key substance in the [[Chemical industry|chemical industry]]. Output was about 261 million metric tons in 2024. It is also the electrolyte in lead-acid batteries.

Family of medium-large coastal [[Seabird|seabirds]], comprising the gannets and boobies. Its 11 species were once placed in the genus *Sula*, but gannets (*Morus*) and true boobies (*Sula*) can be told apart, and Abbott's booby has its own genus. Sulids plunge-dive from the air for fish and similar prey, with streamlined, "torpedo-shaped" bodies that reduce [[Drag (physics)|drag]]. Their webbed feet connect all four toes, and their nostrils lie inside the bill to keep water out. They measure about 60 to 85 cm (24 to 33 in) long. Sulids breed in colonies; gannets lay one egg, and boobies usually lay two or three. They are not truly pelagic like the related [[Procellariiformes]] and usually stay near coasts.

Roman general and statesman of the late [[Roman Republic]], dictator from 82 BC. He rose to prominence through campaigns against Jugurtha, Germanic tribes, and Italian allies in the Social War. As consul in 88 BC, he marched his army on [[Rome]], the first late-republican general to do so and win a civil war. After purging his opponents, he revived the office of dictator and reformed constitutional law to restore the primacy of the Senate and limit the power of the tribunes. He then resigned his dictatorship and retired. His use of force for political power set a precedent for [[Pompey]] and [[Julius Caesar]].

Third sultan of Mataram in central Java, reigning 1613–1645. A skilled soldier, he conquered neighboring states and expanded Mataram to its greatest territorial power. He took Wirasaba in 1615, Tuban in 1619 and Madura in 1624. After five years of war he captured [[Surabaya]] in 1625, bringing central and eastern Java under his rule. Mataram's economy depended on agriculture, and Sultan Agung saw little need for a navy. In 1629 his siege of the Dutch base at [[Jakarta]] failed, as the [[Dutch East India Company|Dutch]] had superior naval power. Dutch writers called him Agoeng de Grote, and he was declared a National Hero of Indonesia on November 3, 1975.

Turco-Persian Sunni Muslim state in [[Anatolia]], 1077–1308. Its name Rum meant the medieval [[Roman Empire]] and its peoples, and the state is considered the beginning of Turkish history in Anatolia. Seceding from the [[Seljuk Empire]] under Suleiman ibn Qutalmish in 1077, it was built on Byzantine territory conquered after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071. Its capital was first Nicaea, then Iconium. At its height in the late 12th and early 13th centuries it took Byzantine ports on the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts and reached Lake Van. Its Seljuk sultans bore the brunt of the [[Crusades]], then were defeated by the Mongols at Köse Dağ in 1243 and became vassals of the [[Ilkhanate]]. After the last vassal sultan was murdered in 1308, Anatolian beyliks emerged, among them the Ottoman dynasty, which later reunited Anatolia as the [[Ottoman Empire]].

Any of roughly 35 species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the genus *Rhus* and related genera, in the cashew and mango family. Not to be confused with poison sumac. The culinary species *Rhus coriaria* is ground into a tangy spice prized in Middle Eastern cuisine. Sumac is also used as a dye, as a source of [[Tannin|tannin]] for leather, and in holistic remedies. It has symbolic significance on the Haft-sin table at [[Nowruz]], the Persian New Year. Plants grow in subtropical and temperate regions on nearly every continent except Antarctica and South America.
